### Q10

Address the values of each of the variables Update the dataset to account for these values for the remainder of the questions in this part.

```{r}


Q10 <- brf |>
  select(POORHLTH, MAXDRNKS, SMOKE100, PERSDOC2)

Q10 <- Q10 |>
  select(POORHLTH, MAXDRNKS, SMOKE100, PERSDOC2) |>
 mutate(POORHLTH = case_when(
  POORHLTH == 88 ~ 0,
  TRUE ~ POORHLTH)
  ) |>
  mutate(SMOKE100 = ifelse(SMOKE100 == '1', #assigning levels
          1, 0)) |>
  mutate(PERSDOC2 = ifelse(PERSDOC2 == '1', #assigning levels
          1, 0)) |>
    as.data.frame()
  

#I created a dataframe with my selected variables and assigned values then assigned this to Q10
```


The variables POORHLTH, MAXDRNKS, SMOKE100 are utilized to predict the outcome variable PERSDOC2. 

For POORHLTH, a quantitative variable, we are looking at how many days over the past 30 days respondents reported poor physical or mental health keeping them from doing their usual daily activities. Values 1-30 are counted as number of days. Value '77' which in the Codebook is labeled as 'Don't know/Not sure' will not be counted. Value '88' will be equal to 0. Those who refused, value '99', will be omitted. Frequency of values 1-30: 96,094. 

For MAXDRNKS, another quantitative variable, respondents were asked what was the largest number of alcoholic beverages they had on any occasion during the past 30 days. Values 1-76 are number of drinks with no value changes, while value '77' labeled as 'Don't Know/Not sure' and those that refused (labeled '99') will be omitted.

SMOKE100 is a categorical predictor variable where respondents were asked if they have smoked 100 cigarettes over the course of their life. Value '1' is labeled 'Yes' and assigned to group 1. Value '2' is labeled 'No' and assigned to group 0. Value '7' labeled as Don't Know/Unsure will be labeled as NA as well as value '9' which were refusals. 

For the chosen outcome variable, PERSDOC2, the categorical variable records whether or not respondents have a primary care health provider. Having a primary care provider or not. We are predicting this outcome based on the inputs of the predictor variables POORHLTH, MAXDRINKS, PHYSHLTH. Values '1' and '2' are both equal to 'Yes' and labeled group 1. Value '3' is 'No' and is labeled group 0. Values '7' and '9' will be ommitted as they are non- answers/refusal. This variable will be predicted, meaning predicting whether or not a person has a primary care healthcare provider based on the information/input of the predictor variables.


### Q11

Remove any outliers for each applicable variable. Make sure you are updating the dataset from Q10 and using this dataset for the remainder. 

```{r}
# CG Q11 # 

##Evaluating outliers for POORHLTH
Q11 <- Q10

length(Q11$POORHLTH) 
#observing length of POORHLTH variable:                               441,456

#1.5(IQR) method
upper_lvl <- quantile(Q11$POORHLTH, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) + (1.5 * IQR(Q11$POORHLTH, na.rm = TRUE)) #setting upper level/fence to                   remove values above this value

lower_lvl <- quantile(Q11$POORHLTH, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE) - (1.5 * IQR(Q11$POORHLTH, na.rm = TRUE)) 
#setting lower level/fence to remove values below this value 

#ph_iqr <- Q11 |>
  #select(POORHLTH) |>
  #filter(POORHLTH >= upper_lvl,
         #POORHLTH <= lower_lvl)

## 1.5(IQR) rule was not appropriate for POORHLTH variable

  #observing new observation number after removing outliers; since more than 20%, will try 3SD rule

# using 3SD rule 
lower_bound <- quantile(Q11$POORHLTH, 0.0015, na.rm = TRUE)
upper_bound <- quantile(Q11$POORHLTH, 0.9985, na.rm = TRUE)

Q11 <- Q11 |>
  select(POORHLTH, MAXDRNKS, SMOKE100, PERSDOC2) |>
  filter(
    POORHLTH >= lower_bound,
    POORHLTH <= upper_bound
  )
#POORHLTH after using 3SD rule  

#observing length after removing POORHLTH outliers
ph_out <- Q11 |>
select(POORHLTH) |>
nrow()

##Evaluating outliers for MAXDRINKS 

length(Q11$MAXDRNKS) #441,456 observations                            for variable MAXDRINKS
## using 3SD rule 

lower <- quantile(Q11$MAXDRNKS, 0.0015, na.rm = TRUE)

upper <- quantile(Q11$MAXDRNKS, 0.9985, na.rm = TRUE)


#using 1.5(IQR) rule
upper_fence <- quantile(Q11$MAXDRNKS, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) + (1.5 * IQR(Q11$MAXDRNKS, na.rm = TRUE))

lower_fence <- quantile(Q11$MAXDRNKS, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE) - (1.5 * IQR(Q11$MAXDRNKS, na.rm = TRUE))

Q11 <- Q11 |>
  select(POORHLTH, MAXDRNKS, SMOKE100, PERSDOC2) |>
  filter(
    MAXDRNKS >= lower_fence,
    MAXDRNKS <= upper_fence
  )

length(Q11$MAXDRNKS)
#
#saved new dataframe after removing to Q11 
```


I did not check for outliers for the variable PERSDOC2 as is not applicable as a categorical variable with only two options/groups of 0 or 1. This is the same reasoning for variable SMOKE100. For the quantitative predictor variables of POORHLTH, MAXDRINKS, and PHYSHLTH I tested out both the 1.5(IQR) and 3SD rule. I then evaluated which method was most appropriate by evaluating how many observations were removed. For example, for the POORHLTH variable, over a quarter of values were removed using the 1.5IQR method. Because the 3SD rule is more resistant to outliers, this is the method used to prevent removing too many values. For MAXDRNKS I used the 1.5IQR as this variable is valued on the lower end so I needed more resistance to extreme/higher values.

"Summary()" gives us a five number summary which includes the first quartile, median, third quartile, and the maximum as well as the mean, which provides the average of the values. These values help evaluate and analyze the spread of data. I also used var() in order to evaluate the variance among the variables MAXDRNKS and POORHLTH to provide more information that will provide context when looking at relationships and correlation. I also evaluated the mode to compare amounts of those that do vs do not have a primary care providor and those that have or have not smoked 100 packs in their lifetime.    




```{r}
### Do not edit the following line. It is used by CodeGrade.
# CG Q14 # 

### TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW ###

## Regression predicting PERSDOC2 from POORHLTH and SMOKE100

Q14_modela <- Q11 |>
  select(PERSDOC2, POORHLTH, SMOKE100)
  
Q14a <- glm(PERSDOC2 ~ POORHLTH + SMOKE100, binomial(), Q14_modela)

modela_summary <- summary(Q14a)

## Regression and summary with all three predictor variables 
Q14_modelb <- Q11 |>
  select(PERSDOC2, MAXDRNKS, POORHLTH, SMOKE100) 
  
Q14b <- glm(PERSDOC2 ~ MAXDRNKS + POORHLTH + SMOKE100, binomial(), Q14_modelb) 

modelb_summary <- summary(Q14b)



Q14 <- Q14b 

```


For the regressions in Q14a and b, I analyzed and compared the AIC values and logistic models for each. I evaluated coefficients as well in order to analyze significance. I assigned the second model to Q14 to identify this as the best model. This model had an AIC value of 100780, while Q14a evaluating POORHLTH and SMOKE100 had an AIC of 101806.
